title: In 1942–43 the German occupiers forced about 5,000 Jewish men in Tunisia into labour camps
body: Tunisia, a French protectorate, was under German occupation for six months, from 9 November 1942 until Tunis was freed on 7 May 1943. About 90,000 Jews lived there, says the [Mémorial de la Shoah](https://www.memorialdelashoah.org/en/evenements-expositions/commemorations/souvenir-de-rafl-e-de-tunis-9-decembre-1942.html). With the army came an SS unit under Walter Rauff, developer of the gas vans used to murder Jews in eastern Europe. Community leaders were arrested; on 6 December Rauff demanded 2,000 workers (some accounts say 3,000), and on 9 December the SS rounded up men in Tunis. The community's leaders were made to run a committee that recruited them. About 5,000 men were sent to forced labour in 32 to about 40 camps, many near the front, by the counts of the Mémorial and the [US Holocaust Memorial Museum](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/labor-and-internment-camps-in-north-africa). Jews also faced fines, confiscations, hostage-taking and, in some towns, a yellow star. As the [Montreal Holocaust Museum](https://museeholocauste.ca/en/resources-training/the-holocaust-in-tunisia/) puts it, time, resources and the course of the war limited what the SS could do.

slides.question: German forces began to arrive in Tunis on 9 November 1942. For how many days did they hold the city?
slides.explanation: 179 days: British troops entered Tunis on 7 May 1943. Forced labour for Jewish men had begun five months earlier, in December 1942.

slides.alt: Animation in night blue: a calendar of the 179 days of German occupation fills square by square from 9 November 1942. Paper notices show the SS order of 6 December and the roundup of 9 December; plain figures stand for about 5,000 forced labourers; a candle; then 7 May 1943, Tunis freed.

slides.prompt: Drag through the calendar of the occupation. Find the day Tunis was freed, and read how long the forced labour had lasted.
slides.takeaway: 7 May 1943, day 179 of the occupation. The order for workers had come on 6 December 1942, 152 days earlier: about five months of forced labour for some 5,000 men.

slides.heading: Made to organise it
slides.text: Under threat, the community's own leaders, its president Moïse Borgel and the lawyer Paul Ghez among them, had to run a committee that drew up the lists of workers. Both men published their accounts in 1943 and 1944, and the historian Haïm Saadoun notes that they do not always agree.

slides.question: When the SS demanded Jewish workers in occupied Tunis in December 1942, who was made to draw up the lists?
slides.explanation: The community's leaders, under threat, ran a recruitment committee. About 5,000 men were sent to forced labour before Tunis was freed on 7 May 1943.
